lead: This unit is about the instruments that measure blood pressure, blood flow, heart sounds and breathing. After it you can read a sphygmomanometer or a dilution curve, explain what a phonocardiograph records, and work out lung volumes and airway resistance from a spirometer or a plethysmograph.
about: The unit covers the instruments that measure the body's two transport systems. 2.1 starts with arterial pressure, taken directly by catheter and indirectly by cuff and Korotkoff sounds. 2.2 moves to flow, using dye and thermal dilution to get cardiac output. 2.3 reads the mechanical events of the heart as sound, and 2.4 applies the same ideas to the foetus and to rhythm alarms. The second half is the lungs: 2.5 measures volumes with a spirometer, 2.6 measures flow and the pressures around the alveoli, 2.7 watches oxygen and breathing at the bedside, and 2.8 closes the loop with the body plethysmograph, which gives the volumes and resistances a spirometer alone cannot reach.

chapters.idea: Blood pressure is a pressure difference between artery and atmosphere, and it can be read either by putting a sensor inside the artery or by watching how a cuff on the arm changes the flow below it.
chapters.depth: Direct method: needle or cannula in the radial artery, saline-filled catheter, strain-gauge (Statham P23 type) transducer, bridge amplifier, recorder; zeroing at the right atrium, the catheter's natural frequency and damping, and why a bubble in the line flattens the trace. Indirect method: Riva-Rocci cuff, mercury and aneroid manometers, the auscultatory method with Korotkoff phases I to V, phase IV muffling versus phase V disappearance, palpatory and Doppler/ultrasound methods, and the automated oscillometric method which records the pressure of maximum cuff oscillation as mean arterial pressure. Errors from cuff width (bladder about 40% of arm circumference), arm level and deflation rate. Only a few universities examine catheter dynamic response; most examine Korotkoff and oscillometry.

figure.title: Auscultatory blood pressure measurement
figure.aria: Cuff deflation produces Korotkoff sounds that are picked up, amplified and read off as the systolic and diastolic pressures.

chapters.example: A 12 cm cuff on an arm of 28 cm circumference is inflated to 160 mmHg and let down at 3 mmHg/s. Korotkoff sounds appear at 128 mmHg, become muffled at 100 mmHg and disappear at 82 mmHg. (a) Give systolic, diastolic and mean arterial pressure. (b) Express systolic pressure in kPa. (c) An arterial catheter in the same patient reads 132/86 mmHg. Why is it different? Answer: (a) systolic 128 mmHg, diastolic 82 mmHg (phase V); pulse pressure = 128 − 82 = 46 mmHg, so MAP = 82 + 46/3 = 97.3 mmHg. (b) 1 mmHg = 0.1333 kPa, so 128 × 0.1333 = 17.1 kPa. (c) The cuff measures pressure in the tissue around the artery, and the reading depends on cuff width, arm position and deflation rate, so the indirect value is a few mmHg lower than the intra-arterial one.
chapters.trap: Writing phase IV (muffling, 100 mmHg) as the diastolic value when the examiner wants phase V, and forgetting that a cuff that is too narrow reads falsely high.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1: physiological transducers, the strain-gauge load cell, bio-amplifiers and recording systems.
chapters.leave: Electrode theory and ECG lead placement to Unit 1; pacemakers, defibrillators and the heart-lung machine to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: Cardiac output is the volume the heart pushes out per minute, and dilution methods find it by injecting a known amount of indicator and measuring how fast the blood carries it past a downstream sensor.
chapters.depth: The Fick principle as the reference. Indicator (dye) dilution: Stewart-Hamilton equation CO = 60·I/A, indocyanine green, densitometer on the arterial line, the first-pass concentration curve, recirculation, exponential extrapolation of the downslope, area measurement by planimetry or digitising, injection and sampling sites. Thermal dilution: cold saline or dextrose, thermistor-tipped pulmonary artery (Swan-Ganz) catheter, the computation constant K supplied with the catheter, why the area is a temperature-time integral, why iced injectate gives a larger signal, why it is safer and repeatable. Only a few universities derive the Stewart-Hamilton equation; most ask for the equation with units and one calculation. The blood cell counter listed with this topic is taught in Unit 3.

figure.aria: The dye concentration rises sharply after injection and decays almost exponentially; the area under this first-pass curve is the denominator of the Stewart-Hamilton equation.

chapters.example: 5 mg of indocyanine green is injected and the arterial concentration curve is recorded. The computed area under the first pass is 60 mg·s/L. (a) Find the cardiac output. (b) What would it be if the area were 50 mg·s/L? Answer: (a) CO = 60 × I / A = 60 × 5 / 60 = 5 L/min. (b) 60 × 5 / 50 = 6 L/min, so cardiac output is inversely proportional to the area under the curve.
chapters.trap: Dropping the factor 60 when converting seconds to minutes, and including the recirculation hump in the area instead of extrapolating the downslope.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1: transducers and bio-amplifiers; the heart rate and cardiac cycle ideas from Unit 1.
chapters.leave: The Fick principle as an oxygen-consumption method to Unit 3 blood gas analysis; the Swan-Ganz catheter as a bedside procedure is described only at block level.

chapters.idea: The heart makes low-frequency sound when its valves snap shut, and a stethoscope or a microphone with the right filter can record that sound and time it against the ECG.
chapters.depth: Origin and timing of S1 (mitral and tricuspid closure) and S2 (aortic and pulmonary closure), S3 and S4, frequency content roughly 20-600 Hz with murmurs higher. Stethoscope: bell for low frequencies, diaphragm for higher, tubing length and bore, why it couples sound to the ear rather than amplifying it. Phonocardiograph: air-coupled or contact microphone, preamplifier, band-pass filter, amplifier, recorder or display, simultaneous ECG channel as a time reference, A2-P2 splitting, systolic and diastolic murmurs on the trace, heart rate from interval measurement.

figure.title: Phonocardiograph signal chain
figure.aria: Heart sound is picked up at the chest, converted to an electrical signal, filtered to the heart-sound band, amplified and recorded alongside the ECG.

chapters.example: A phonocardiogram is recorded with a 25-400 Hz filter together with lead II ECG. S1 begins 0.05 s after the R wave, S2 begins 0.35 s after the same R wave, and the next R wave comes 0.80 s later. (a) Find the systolic interval. (b) Find the heart rate. (c) Would a 600 Hz murmur appear on this trace? Answer: (a) 0.35 − 0.05 = 0.30 s. (b) RR = 0.80 s, so rate = 60/0.80 = 75 beats per minute; diastolic interval = 0.80 − 0.30 = 0.50 s. (c) No. 600 Hz lies above the 400 Hz cutoff, so it is attenuated heavily by the filter and does not show.
chapters.trap: Saying S2 is caused by valve opening. Both S1 and S2 come from valve closure, and S2 is the aortic and pulmonary valves shutting at the end of systole.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1: ECG recording, bio-amplifiers and filter basics.
chapters.leave: The ECG machine itself, lead systems and vectorcardiography to Unit 1; valve disease and surgery are not examined here.

chapters.idea: Two bedside monitors watch a rhythm: the foetal monitor separates the baby's heartbeat from the mother's, and the arrhythmia monitor measures each RR interval and shouts when it goes outside set limits.
chapters.depth: Foetal monitoring: abdominal ultrasound Doppler for heart rate, abdominal ECG with maternal QRS cancellation by subtraction or logic, direct scalp electrode for the foetal ECG, intrauterine pressure catheter for contractions, the cardiotocograph trace and its baseline rate (110-160 beats per minute), beat-to-beat variability, accelerations, and early, variable and late decelerations. Foetal phonocardiography as the sound-based alternative. Arrhythmia monitoring: QRS detection, RR interval measurement, instantaneous rate, tachycardia, bradycardia, pause and asystole limits, alarm circuits, artefact rejection and why a missed beat doubles one interval. Holter and event recorders are in Unit 1; defibrillation is in Unit 5.

figure.aria: Three RR intervals are measured beat by beat; the third is twice the normal length, so the monitor flags it as a pause and alarms.

chapters.example: A cardiotocograph on a mother at 38 weeks shows a baseline foetal heart rate of 140 beats per minute, variability of ±5 beats per minute, and a fall to 90 beats per minute that begins 20 s after the peak of a contraction and lasts 40 s. (a) Name the deceleration. (b) How long is one foetal RR interval at baseline? (c) The ward arrhythmia monitor alarms when an RR interval exceeds 1.5 s; it records 1.60 s. What rate does it report? Answer: (a) It starts after the contraction, so it is a late deceleration, a sign of poor placental blood flow. (b) 60/140 = 0.429 s = 429 ms. (c) Instantaneous rate = 60/1.60 = 37.5 beats per minute, far below the limit, so the pause alarm sounds.
chapters.trap: Reading the mother's ECG as the foetal rate, and forgetting that a monitor that computes rate from single RR intervals halves the reported rate when one foetal beat is missed.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2.3 for heart sounds and phonocardiography; Unit 1 for ECG recording and the heart rate monitor.
chapters.leave: Holter and event recorders and ECG troubleshooting to Unit 1; pacemakers, defibrillators and ablation to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: A spirometer records how much air moves in and out of the lungs and how fast, and the shape of that record separates a blocked airway from a stiff lung.
chapters.depth: Spirometer types: water-sealed bell, dry rolling seal, turbine and pneumotachograph-based; the 3 L calibration syringe; BTPS correction (37 °C, saturated with water vapour) and why volumes are quoted BTPS. Primary volumes (tidal volume, inspiratory and expiratory reserve volumes, residual volume) and capacities (inspiratory capacity, vital capacity, functional residual capacity, total lung capacity). The forced vital capacity manoeuvre, its spirogram, FEV1, FEV1/FVC ratio, forced expiratory flow 25-75%, peak expiratory flow rate, and the flow-volume loop. Obstructive versus restrictive patterns; helium dilution and nitrogen washout named only, because residual volume is measured in Chapter 2.8.

figure.aria: The normal spirogram climbs to 4 L and reaches 3.2 L in the first second; the obstructive trace rises slowly and reaches only 1.2 L in that second.

chapters.example: A healthy man gives FVC = 4.0 L and FEV1 = 3.2 L. A patient with asthma gives FVC = 3.0 L and FEV1 = 1.2 L. (a) Compute FEV1/FVC for each. (b) Classify the patient. (c) The patient's peak flow is 400 L/min; convert it to L/s. Answer: (a) Healthy: 3.2/4.0 = 0.80, that is 80%. Patient: 1.2/3.0 = 0.40, that is 40%. (b) The ratio is below the 0.70 cutoff with a low FEV1, so this is an obstructive pattern. (c) 400/60 = 6.67 L/s.
chapters.trap: Using FEV1 alone instead of the FEV1/FVC ratio, and forgetting that a spirometer can never measure residual volume, because that air never leaves the lungs.
chapters.prereq: None beyond school physics; the volume-time idea is built from scratch.
chapters.leave: Residual volume, functional residual capacity and airway resistance to Chapter 2.8; blood gas analysers and pH to Unit 3; ventilators and their modes to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: Air flow is measured as the small pressure drop across a known resistance, and the pressures inside and around the alveoli are measured to see how hard the breathing muscles are working.
chapters.depth: Pneumotachometer: Fleisch capillary bundle giving laminar (Poiseuille) flow, screen and hot-wire types, differential pressure transducer across the resistance, the relation flow = pressure drop / resistance, linearity limits when flow becomes turbulent, and integration of the flow signal to get volume with drift correction. Pressures: intra-alveolar (mouth pressure with the shutter closed or a catheter), intrapleural (oesophageal balloon), transpulmonary and transthoracic pressures; units cm H2O, with 1 cm H2O = 0.098 kPa; typical resting intrapleural pressure about −5 cm H2O and alveolar pressure about 0 to ±1 cm H2O; the role of airway resistance in linking flow and pressure. Only a few universities derive the Poiseuille relation; most ask the sensitivity and the pressure arithmetic.

figure.title: Pneumotachometer and pressure measurement
figure.aria: Air passing through the mesh creates a pressure drop that a differential transducer converts to flow, and the flow signal is integrated to give volume.

chapters.example: A Fleisch pneumotachograph gives a differential pressure of 0.75 cm H2O at a steady flow of 0.5 L/s. (a) Find its sensitivity. (b) The flow is integrated over a 1 s inspiration with average flow 0.5 L/s; find the tidal volume. (c) If airway resistance is 2 cm H2O per L/s and mouth pressure is 0, find the alveolar pressure; and if intrapleural pressure is −5 cm H2O, find the transpulmonary pressure. Answer: (a) 0.75/0.5 = 1.5 cm H2O per L/s. (b) 0.5 × 1 = 0.5 L. (c) Alveolar pressure = mouth pressure + resistance × flow = 0 + 2 × 0.5 = 1 cm H2O. Transpulmonary pressure = 1 − (−5) = 6 cm H2O.
chapters.trap: Mixing gauge and absolute pressures, and forgetting that the pneumotachometer is linear only while the flow stays laminar.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2.5 for lung volumes; Unit 1 for the differential pressure transducer and carrier amplifier.
chapters.leave: Airway resistance measurement and the plethysmograph to Chapter 2.8; ventilator pressure modes and alarms to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: Oxygen saturation is read from how much red and infrared light the pulsing arterial blood absorbs, and breathing is watched from how much the chest impedance changes with each breath.
chapters.depth: Pulse oximetry: Beer-Lambert law, absorption of oxygenated and reduced haemoglobin at about 660 nm (red) and 940 nm (infrared), light-emitting diodes and photodiode across a finger or earlobe, splitting each channel into AC (pulsatile) and DC (tissue) parts, the ratio R = (AC/DC red)/(AC/DC infrared), the empirical calibration curve that turns R into SpO2, and the limits: saturation is not ventilation, so a patient on oxygen can look normal while breathing badly; motion, low perfusion, nail polish and carboxyhaemoglobin cause errors. Impedance pneumography: two or four electrodes on the chest, a small alternating current at about 50 kHz, transthoracic impedance rising with air in the lungs (roughly 1 Ω per litre), bridge and band-pass amplifier, respiration waveform, artefact from chest movement and from the cardiac stroke. Apnoea monitor: alarms when no impedance change larger than a set amount occurs for 10-20 s, used for neonates in hospital and at home. Oximetry is not named in some of the syllabi for this unit; it completes the bedside measurement set.

figure.title: Pulse oximeter signal path
figure.aria: Two light-emitting diodes shine through the finger, the photodiode measures the transmitted light, and the pulsatile-to-steady ratio of the two channels is converted to a saturation reading.

chapters.example: A finger probe gives red channel DC = 100 units and AC = 2 units, infrared channel DC = 110 units and AC = 4 units. (a) Compute R. (b) The calibration table maps R = 0.55 to about 98%; which way does R move if saturation falls? (c) An apnoea monitor shows a 0.5 Ω impedance change with a 500 mL breath; find its sensitivity. Answer: (a) R = (2/100)/(4/110) = 0.02/0.0364 = 0.55. (b) Less oxygenated blood absorbs more red light, so the red AC/DC term grows and R rises; the table then reads a lower saturation. (c) 0.5 Ω / 0.5 L = 1 Ω per litre.
chapters.trap: Believing a normal SpO2 means good breathing. Saturation says nothing about carbon dioxide or respiratory effort, so apnoea must be detected by impedance or by capnography.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2.5 and 2.6 for breathing volumes and flow; Unit 1 for bio-amplifiers and bridge circuits.
chapters.leave: Blood gas analysis and pH electrodes to Unit 3; oxygen sensors based on electrochemical transducers to Unit 4; ventilator alarms to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: Inside a sealed box, the small pressure changes made by panting against a shutter give the gas volume in the chest by Boyle's law, and the pressure changes during free breathing give airway resistance.
chapters.depth: Whole-body plethysmograph: sealed box of about 600 L, mouth shutter, box pressure transducer, mouth pressure transducer, panting at about 1 Hz so that compression and expansion stay adiabatic in the box and isothermal in the lungs, Boyle's law P1V1 = P2V2, thoracic gas volume V_tg = V_box × ΔP_box/ΔP_mouth, functional residual capacity, then residual volume = FRC − expiratory reserve volume and total lung capacity = residual volume + vital capacity; BTPS and water-vapour correction, the 47 mmHg water vapour pressure. Airway resistance: shutter open, alveolar pressure taken from box pressure through a calibration factor, resistance = pressure difference / flow, specific airway conductance as resistance in inverse litres. Normal resistance is roughly 0.6 to 2.4 cm H2O per L/s. Only a few universities teach specific conductance; most ask the V_tg and resistance calculations.

figure.title: Plethysmograph measurement
figure.aria: Panting against a closed shutter produces a box pressure and a mouth pressure whose ratio, scaled by box volume, gives thoracic gas volume and hence residual volume.

chapters.example: A subject sits in a 600 L plethysmograph. With the shutter closed he pants; mouth pressure swings by 10 cm H2O and box pressure by 0.05 cm H2O. (a) Find the thoracic gas volume. (b) His expiratory reserve volume is 1.2 L and slow vital capacity is 4.0 L; find residual volume and total lung capacity. (c) With the shutter open, a flow of 2 L/s gives a box pressure swing equal to 4 cm H2O of alveolar pressure; find airway resistance. Answer: (a) V_tg = V_box × ΔP_box/ΔP_mouth = 600 × 0.05/10 = 3.0 L, which is the functional residual capacity. (b) Residual volume = 3.0 − 1.2 = 1.8 L; total lung capacity = 1.8 + 4.0 = 5.8 L. (c) Resistance = 4/2 = 2 cm H2O per L/s, a mildly raised value.
chapters.trap: Forgetting the water-vapour correction and BTPS conditions, and treating the box pressure as alveolar pressure without the calibration factor between them.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2.5 for vital capacity and the volume names, and Chapter 2.6 for flow and airway resistance.
chapters.leave: Spirometry detail and the forced manoeuvre to Chapter 2.5; ventilator therapy to Unit 5.

links: pressure in the arteries and flow through them describe the same circulation
